newsitem.title: FRANCE: Iraq's Aziz, in France, raps U.S, Britain.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's Aziz, in France, raps U.S, Britain.

text.p: Iraqi Vice-Prime Minister Tareq Aziz praised France on Monday for breaking ranks with the United States and Britain against their former Gulf War foe and accused Washington and London of pursuing a vendetta against Baghdad.

After talks with French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, Aziz told reporters his country was complying fully with U.N. Security Council resolutions arising from Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which led to the 1991 Gulf War, and the Council should now consider a full lifting of its economic embargo.

"The problem is biased policy by the United States and the United Kingdom against Iraq for reasons which have nothing to do with the text of the (U.N.) resolutions but for their own political reasons," he said.
"France doesn't have that special agenda against Iraq."

On his first visit since December 1995, Aziz thanked France for pulling out of the western coalition patrolling the airspace over northern Iraq. Paris took the decision last month, citing the fact that the patrols were no longer linked to a humanitarian relief operation for the Kurds.
He said his one-hour meeting with Juppe had been very useful in developing understanding.

"I made it clear to Mr Juppe...that the main problem for Iraq is not the implementation of the U.N. resolutions. We do not conceal anything. We have implemented all the essential elements of the resolutions and...the Security Council is bound to look seriously at the lifting of the embargo," he said.
France was doing its best to help Iraq "in the good, honest, balanced legal implementation of the U.N. resolutions", he said.

France recently campaigned for the implementation of a U.N. oil-for-food resolution and has stressed that if Baghdad fully complies with all the Gulf War resolutions, the international community must not maintain the embargo simply because it does not like President Saddam Hussein.

Two French oil companies, Elf-Aquitaine and Total, are taking part in the supervised oil sales and have signed long-term deals with Baghdad to help modernise the Iraqi oil industry once the sanctions are lifted.
However the Foreign Ministry said on Sunday there was no question of Saddam's son Uday being admitted to France for medical treatment following an attempt on his life last month.
